newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish opposition wants consultations on 98 budget.
newsitem.headline: Polish opposition wants consultations on 98 budget.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity Election Action (AWS) alliance, which hopes to defeat ruling ex-communists in September general elections, demanded on Monday to be consulted by the government on its 1998 budget draft.

Marian Krzaklewski, Solidarity chairman and a leader of the group of more than 30 small rightist parties centred around the trade union, said AWS would make amendments in the draft now being prepared by the finance ministry, if it won the polls.
"The concept of the budget should be subject to consultations...because it is not known who will govern in Poland next year," Krzaklewski told reporters.
But he said AWS agreed with some elements of the draft.

"I would see a possibility of consultations on the level of experts and not politicians...It would be necessary to explain mutual divergencies because it is not the case that we differ in everything," he added.
Government spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska rejected the suggestion of consultations with the government but said parliamentary committees would be free to consult AWS or any other experts.

"It is the responsibility of the government to present the budget. The parliamentary committees, if they decide that it is necessary, will certainly invite experts (but) the government will present the budget as it is obliged to do," she said.
Krzaklewski said that if his group formed the government it would seek to give more money to local governments to reduce the central administration's role in public spending.

He declined to comment on whether Solidarity supported Finance Minister Marek Belka's central plan to cut next year's budget deficit to 1.9 percent of gross domestic product from 2.8 percent planned for 1997.
The minister argues the cut is necessary to cool booming domestic demand, while the central bank says the tightening should be deeper to get trade and current account deficits under control.
Krzaklewski criticised the leader of the co-ruling Polish Peasant Party (PSL), Waldemar Pawlak, for demanding more spending on agriculture at the expense of a higher deficit.
"These are pre-election discussions...Pawlak wants to be able tell the farmers that he gave them something by increasing farm spending at a cost of a higher deficit," he said.

The Peasants have proposed that the deficit be kept at least at this year's level -- an idea rejected by the finance minister, who vowed last week to resist any pressure from parties campaigning for parliamentary elections.
The ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), whose Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz backs the finance ministry, can outvote the Peasants during cabinet sessions.
Under Polish law, Solidarity, if it forms a government, will be able to propose amendments to the budget draft submitted by Cimoszewicz's cabinet.

Solidarity, whose many members helped defeat communist rule in 1989, is running neck-and-neck with the ex-communists, each supported by more than 20 percent. The balance of power in the next parliament will probably be held by smaller parties.
